title: Encapsulation & UML
description: Hiding complexity, guarding data, and reading UML diagrams.

questions.explanation: cash is private but getCash() is public — the getter is the legal way in.

options: balance is public — anyone can set it to anything
questions.explanation: A public field has no guard. Make it private and validate inside withdraw().

questions.prompt: Order the UML compartments top to bottom.
questions.explanation: Name on top, fields in the middle, methods at the bottom.

questions.prompt: In UML, which symbol marks a private member?
questions.explanation: Minus = private, plus = public, hash = protected.

questions.prompt: Match each UML symbol to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Plus, minus, hash, underline — the four symbols you read most.

questions.prompt: This UML box — which Java matches it?
questions.code:
Player
-----------
- score : int
+ addPoints(p : int) : void
questions.explanation: Minus → private field, plus → public method. The symbols translate directly.
20 + 1 + 1 = 22. The private field only changes through the public method.

questions.prompt: The UML says the field is private. What's wrong?
options: The code declares it public, contradicting the UML
Nothing — UML is just a suggestion
questions.explanation: The diagram is the design contract: minus means the code must say private.

questions.prompt: Hiding internal details behind a simple interface is called ___.
questions.code: // ___ : show the what, hide the how
questions.explanation: Abstraction = show the what, hide the how. (And yes — that first clause was a trap.)

questions.prompt: Which Java matches this JavaScript encapsulation?
questions.explanation: JS #code (truly private) maps to Java's private field — same guard, different syntax.
